04/06/2017
What are you not
 
	I’m a little teapot short and stout. I’m also not very honest. Note here that I have avoided the Epimenides paradox by not claiming that I always lie. Everybody lies, as much as everybody dies. I think that the ninth commandment was poorly thought out, like rules parents make for their first child- well meant, but without any thought to realism. Either that or God really didn’t want real estate prices in heaven going up. Being priced out of heaven by humans would be too much of a hilarious straight shooting comedy for Jesus after all.
	But even in this sad cesspool of sin, something my Catholic school assured me the earth is, I’m particularly bad at observing this particular commandment. Lying comes a little too naturally to me. I’m not sure why. If I had to guess though, I would say that I’m afraid. In fact, I think the main, or perhaps only reason people lie is because they’re afraid. Afraid of rejection, of being found out for the fraud that they think they are, afraid of reality. So according to transitive properties I must lie more than everyone else because I’m more afraid than everyone else.
	Now that took a rather dark turn. But hey, I could be lying. Because what could I possibly be so afraid of? Why should I be more afraid than everyone else? It seems rather presumptuous to say that I’m more afraid. After all the mortality rate of my peer group should be orders of magnitude lower than that of people in Israel, or the middle-eastern countries seemingly constantly at war against … democracy(?), I think is what the media tells me. My mortality rate is so low that I know stupid facts like that eating one-thousand bananas will increase my mortality rate by 1 micromort, meaning that the probability of my death goes up by one millionth. This is rather impressive. I will soon look into buying one thousand bananas. These challenges are really what makes me feel alive. Thrilling.
	Maybe I’m afraid of being dropped, of people finding out that I’m some sort of failure and deciding that I’m not worth their time. So perhaps I’m not very confident. This seems to feel like it has some inkling of truth. Like many deep seated traumas, this one could even be rooted in my childhood. Those moments when I returned home with a bad grade and had to then endure hours of being shouted at, or saying that I wanted to be an artist and having my drawings be mocked. At the very least, modern outlooks on parenting trends seem to agree with me. Look at that, by asking what I’m not, I have seem to started to answer what I am. Well, let’s not dwell in this place too much. The pained confusion of why I’m not confident is much more enjoyable to read than me moaning about why I am unconfident; a rather drab and common topic on internet forums.
	I’m not honest, but I try my best to be genuine. Oddly, I have come to realize more and more that those who live life to the fullest seem to make a habit of being honest. So I don’t think I can live a genuine life without living an honest life. Being afraid of reality and rejection would mean that I can only run and stuff my head in the sand- an idiom that has its roots in ostrich behavior by the way. 
	But I’m pretty sure I’m not an ostrich.
I think I like this answer to this prompt.
I am not an ostrich.

04/14/2017
What happened on that Day?

	It was daytime. It was a warm daytime with sunlight streaming in through glass doors that led out to the balcony and a brilliant Californian day. The fan beat overhead, almost silent, attempting to chase the heat away. I held a heavy book in my hands. It dealt with patricide and Russia, with faith and cynicism, jealousy and honor; my world. It was the world that I had always tried to understand a little more of using the conflicting nature of people shown to us through ageless classics.
	But it was such a nice day outside. I had long forgotten how nice a warm day feels, what it was like to smile only because the sky was blue. The catalyst for this change was a few feet away tapping away at a keyboard, frowning at some probability problem that had to do with efficiently finding the maximum using some kind of random walk. Interesting, terribly complicated, and, according to her, a very fun problem to think about.
	My mind drifted from the book to a conversation we had had yesterday. I wanted things to change, and I wanted somehow to change them. She replied that I was obviously miserable, that I was missing the entire point of being alive. I retorted with a bible parable, her with a story about seagulls. ‘I want to help’ was my stance. ‘But you aren’t free’ was her reply. Maybe that’s why I like reading Dostoevsky, I thought, because his characters seemed caged, angry.
I shifted on the couch, curling into a more comfortable position. The sun sinking into evening… tempting me to close my eyes. My mind was hopelessly scattered now. We had talked about empathy and sympathy. To understand one person IS to sympathize with them! Was her declaration against my point that these were different. I explained that to understand doesn’t mean that you sympathize, because sympathy seems to imply some form of compassion. Yet we can hate ourselves, showing that even in extreme instances of empathy there can be a plausible absence of sympathy. Yes, okay, but why do you care? Because I want to know how we can properly sympathize with each other.  But why?! Because then no one would have to feel hopelessly isolated. Again her signature frown- she was thinking about it. It interested her. A compliment.

My mind kept wandering, always into the same person.

She was the most straightforward person that I had ever met.

It’s so easy to be healthy! You just have to know that you want it and then just do it! Was her take on exercise. ‘But what if I feel lazy?’ I ventured. Then you ARE lazy. It was a merciless response, but fair enough. I started jogging. There was also a laughably convoluted conversation about how cutting carbs would free me from being dictated by hunger, and enable me to pursue what trains of thought I’d want. So of course, I started eating salads. 

I wanted to know what living this straightforward life was like.

	I had been closing a chapter in my life. One written by wanting to be myself in a world that seemed perversely interested in finding ways to kick me down. Such a life, I realized, was defined by staying standing despite everything crushing you, which meant being defined by resilience and a lurking anger. When everything belittles you, anger can keep you up. Anger, idealism, or indifference. But I wasn’t being attacked any more. All my coping mechanisms were doing nothing, all my walls and mirrors protecting me from threats now only imagined, hemming me in. I felt empty, hopelessly weighed down by all these self-made structures that no one could understand. The driving force of anger had burned to nothing, leaving me cold. Why was I here? Who was to blame? I hated it all.
	Well if you don’t like it so much you don’t have to be alive you know! Just get a knife or something and ask if you really want to live, and you do, of course you do! Because you’re alive right?! A challenge that hung in the air, her outburst a little too passionate for the talk we were having. I gave an awkward smile, remembering. A knife, me. No cuts, no dramatic gestures, no plea for attention. Just me, a knife, and a question. The question. I had felt tired, so tired. I said so, her expression softened. We were both talking from experience.
 	We’re here because we want to be. She started. So stop being so damn miserable? I finished. She smiled. Yes. Exactly.

“Arrrgh.”
A frustrated grumble took me out of my dozy memories. I looked over at the small hunched figure with her head in her hands.
“Having trouble?”
“Yes, I’m sure I can figure it out. I just need time to... How’s your book?”
“Interesting, just read a chapter called ‘The Inquisitor’. It’s about how… well… it’s complicated.”
“Tell me.”
I ambled over to the table, collecting my thoughts. Long shadows sprawled across the living room floor, the sun flaring orange for the final hour before it set. She was here for a few more days, then we’ll never see each other again. That was fine. I would miss her, but that was fine as well. We would trade presents, and say our goodbyes, and that was how life flowed by, how people passed by. But today I looked out at a beautiful day and appreciated the sun’s warmth, looked up into a clear sky and smiled at its clarity. It had been a fine day.

Why bother?

	Ah, hello old friend. I hope it’s fair to call a question a friend, since friendship is really only a matter of intimacy. I wonder if there has been a single day in the past decade where you have not taken up at least some corner of my thoughts. Such an incessant friend, so needy, and unrelenting. We’ve been down many paths trying to satiate your need to be answered, your need to be truly understood and satisfied. As is the case with old friends, I feel that I’ve perhaps adopted too many of your mannerisms and your mode of thinking. I’ve spent entire days pondering what you mean. I’ve even let you creep into conversations with my other friends, and the need for an answer grows only stronger with every failure.
	I first really made an acquaintance in the very early years. You make yourself known best when there is something making me do things I do not want to: when there are tests I don’t care about, when I have to perform actions I have no real investment in, and when I find effort to be just too much at certain points in time. So I would get to know you through the times when I was in my room, trying to live the dreams of other people, making myself act stronger than I felt.
	As I grew older I’ve found that you have a lot of friends, lots of people you bothered with your presence. One frenchman even said “There is only one really serious philosophical question, and that is suicide.” Boy you really drove that man up the wall. Remember that time when I thought that life was about what you can leave behind? About the people who will pick up your dreams and keep whatever fire you lit burning towards the ends of eternity? I really did read too much fantasy back in the day. There was also a short stint where I thought life was about being nice to other people and trying to understand them. That was really the bible talking, but it really helped me question morality in interesting ways later down the line. So I guess I salvaged something out of that mess. I had a stage where I thought life was about hope, and about breaking apart everything to grab only whatever happiness I could. I think I was sad then, and your constant questioning of my life choices made me selfish and very angry. It didn’t help that around about this time we thought that life might be about trying to help the people we care about. Figuring out that those same people can hurt you in ways we thought I was already guarded against wasn’t much fun, especially when it happened a few more times. Well, fool me twice I guess.

Myself and the world

The idea exists to be expressed. The thought is the why and what of what we do.

It's an odd way to start off a concept, but I mean that the existence of ideas means the existence of the person. The person is defined by what they think and why they think it. Negatives, positives, empathy, cruelty, faith, disbelief; they're all rooted in thought.

As an extension of this thought, it would be fair to think that the idea is the world. The world is defined by what we think regardless of how the world itself is arranged. The world is indifferent, we just shape it to be cruel or kind. Mind over matter.

The thought leads onto the very basic concept that everyone lives in their own world, completely different from the world of others. Every mind is a world for the world is in the eyes of the beholder.

Doesn't this worry you sometimes? What if that one person you thought was nice to you actually just thought nothing of you? What if those who you thought were significant in your life held you in no significance at all?
Also, on brighter notes, what if people you just passed by everyday perceived so much more beauty in the everyday than you ever did. It could very well be that the stony faced person whom you ridiculed for being one of the herd actually ponders questions that would befuddle you even with the very basic openings of its argument.

The world is acting on you, but at the same time you are acting on the world. You cannot simply be a victim to any whim of fate. A victim of fate is one who resolutely chooses to fall, not one who accepts the fall.
The fall itself is avoidable, but will most probably come with a life of mere existence.

The master of the world is you. To complain has no meaning in such a world. To believe is to make possible. To act is everything. Boldness is magic.

Myself and you

And hello stranger! Here is myself, and there is yourself. Who am I? And who are you? I would much like to tell you who I am, and I would much like to hear who you are.

But how limited our means to do this. All language and art can't cover our whole existence. For my thoughts create a world, and your thoughts your world.
How can we express a world of thoughts with words so untrained? Or with drawings so unpolished? Even with mastery, perhaps I would be able to show you just one instant of thought that I hold precious. If I ever do I only hope that you too will hold this moment precious.

To say that a world exists in one's mind sounds marvelous! Doesn't it quite? To say that 'I'm special because I hold my own world'. But how sad is it at the same time to hold a whole world to yourself. Is it not depressing to think that I live in such isolation from you, and you from me? I'm afraid that my world is rather queer and alien. I hope it does not dissuade you from knowing me.

For I want to be known. I do so very want to be seen. I do so very want to see. What lies past that smiling face that you always put on and what thoughts beyond the 'how are you's and 'I'm doing great thank you!'

Because without this the world is a world of worlds. And in so many worlds one little thought does get rather lonely. Are you not lonely too? So unsure and ill-placed?

Myself and I

Identity, the greatest lie of all. How can I see me from outside myself, when trying to get out leads me back to myself. To try and look at yourself is trying to escape the mobius strip by walking along it. Identity is an infinite trap.
I know myself better than I know anybody, and the infinite alleys and curtains that branch and veil. I am afraid of the dark paths, that is why I have drawn curtains over them.

Yet who but I can call myself by my own highest name? Who else can tread along these winding roads that split and crack and still comfortably call it home?

There are temples here, some broken down, some almost forgotten, all once revered. There are books and books and books strewn about.. on life, on love, on happiness. Scraps of paper desperately torn out after being scribbled on. They were all in search of an answer to a question I don’t know how to say.

I love and hate myself, as I love and hate this world.
This world so full of pain and wonder. Where the glimmering light sometimes refracts into ten thousand thousand shards of light in an instant of purest understanding. This place where it always feels like the tide is rising and I will always drown.

When I act I act upon the world, when the world acts it acts upon me. But here is where I am both world and myself. The quiet tides of this place are tides I have made, the storms, storms I have accepted.

Here I am. Here I always will be.

What do I want?

	What do I want? Well ultimately, I think I want what we all want. I want to be happy. But this is no answer at all.  Perhaps I should move onto a more personal account of happiness. I think that the man who both works at something he believes in and has his work understood is closer to happiness. 
This is still too abstract. Maybe an example might help. 

Imagine a time before art where a person stumbled upon a brick, a crumbling brick in the morning sun surrounded by some slight mold and grass in some corner of the garden. They decided this moment, the most important moment in their life and started about capturing it. But there is no art, bricks were drawn as wonky squares.
This seemed good enough. But this person found that straighter lines would make it seems a little more regular and ‘brick-like’. Which seemed understandable to other people. There is something inherently satisfying about good right angles and clean lines.
But then the person finds this deeply unsatisfying and happens upon that fact that two elongated rectangles on the side makes it seem more… three dimensional somehow.
Now this guy is a nutjob. While what he found may seem true to some people he cares about bricks way too much. But there is more. They find out about shading, then about how there seems to be a line of light on the edge of the darkest edges (as light does ‘bend’ around corners, but how were they to know?). How it is wrong to even draw the outline and to let the colors dictate where a shape starts and ends. One day as he is doing this someone will stop him and say ‘that’s not quite how a brick looks’. It is in this moment that the gap has been closed. Others can now see parts of what the person was trying to create. Their dream, while maybe not quite realized, can finally be shared. One day they might get to show the tranquility of the rough red brick, slightly worn, that was surrounded by soft hues of green and splashed with color from the butterflies and flowers. There is something attractive in this idea. To be able to work on what one loves and finally have people see what is it that one loves about it. 
	Naturally then, the next piece of writing will be the question ‘what is it that I love?’.

Society is constructed. No, that isn’t quite true, as it implied that there is a maniacal, malevolent mind trying to build society brick-by-brick. What I mean to say is that society is a construction.
	By a construction I mean to say that it carries two important qualities: it is artificial, and it is malleable. Society, being artificial, has no hard and fast truths; no absolute values. So all our morals, justice, and freedoms are all just constructs built on abstract nothings. So all of society is malleable, and nothing that is has to be that way. We can change it.
	In the Western consciousness, the Age of Enlightenment and subsequent existentialist philosophies stand as examples of what can be achieved when we realize the shortcomings of the current social narrative on a mass scale. Within a century we distanced ourselves from the monarchies that had been the ruling institutions for the past few millennia, and had created narratives around personal freedoms, rights, and happiness. It is on these ideals that the French Revolution, the Napoleonic wars, and the American Revolution happened. The driving humanist forces behind these movements eventually eroded Christianity, with Nietzsche declaring that “God is dead … and we have killed him”.
Now these themes of truth in science and the general meaningless of life have become the new status quo. But where are we now? The progress of science and economy has brought us this far and helped us get away from religious doctrine and feudalistic societies. But now the themes of the day are a loss of solid moralities, near kafkaesque nightmares of bureaucracy, and marketization of our own attention. We are not the Ubermen that Nietzsche dreamed of, nothing like the absurd heroes of Camus, or the humanists living in good faith that Sartre wanted. We’ve replaced religion with beliefs in science, nationalism, or political parties. Economy has given us scale that can be seen in the aggressive expansion of the village into the metropolis, and the village store, became the national franchise, became the global mega Corp. The everyday man is placed further and further away from any kind of impact or power. All of the promise of democracy is abstracted away to a vote or two every few years backed with rhetoric and little else, with no clear way of seeing how anything impacts anything. Layers and layers of interests create localized mists that block one from seeing anything clearly past a few steps, creating middle management in everything, resulting in more paperwork, more confusion, more drudgery. What’s worse is that it’s not some mastermind villain with an overarching plan that’s doing this to us - it’s just shortsightedness. What seems to make sense in the short term keeps screwing us over in the long term. The built-in apathy towards a system that seems too big to change doesn’t help either.
 The internet came with the promise of a united world with ties to everything, and while it’s done massive good by giving people access to everything, it also gave access to us. Our attention is grabbed and marketed to, everything is a Skinner box that’s designed to induce a limbo-like passivity between our frantic hours of work. The marketing to our tastes divides us more than ever, with so much info spewing out that our overactive brains can make any pattern out of the chaos, and this pattern informs the machines, which then feed us more info to reinforce comfortable patterns. Challenging us creates disruption in user engagement, it’s just easier to keep feeding us the beliefs we already hold.
The above is now becoming pretty obvious, and it’s receiving attention right now. But as with all games, the trick is to play the meta-game. The real problem isn’t that we need single page, easy-to-read tax forms, or that we need to regulate the way the internet hijacks our dopamine seeking brains. The problem is that we need to figure out how to see and interact with the systems that make up our world. Even the world of startups, heralded as the bastion of disruption and innovation, run into these same problems as most of the problems they’re trying to solve these days are just optimization and automation problems. It seems to be mostly fintech, automated delivery, better rental services, etc despite their claims to massive disruption. (So what are we supposed to do? Purchase stocks as we get our food delivered to us in our airbnb to utopia? Like Jesus startups, get your shit together. This is at best zero to point-oh-one). But this is just a symptom of the problem I’m trying to point to. In a world where you can’t see everything, the best most people will try to do is optimize their immediate surroundings to a local maximum. 
What do I mean by meta-game? Well let’s take a brief look at the reality that we live in. We live in a supposed meritocratic capitalist society. None of this is a potshot at meritocracy or capitalism, in fact I’m a big fan. But the ‘supposed’ in supposed meritocratic society comes in when we start measuring for specific performance metrics such as rote memorization, the ability to write to a rubric, or quickly finding mathematical solutions. These are supposedly merits in some sense, but for what? Why? How? We don’t quite know, but we stick numbers to them, and then the massive rat race begins to optimize to maximize these numbers. Capitalism is just this but bigger. Money was supposed to be a tool to help us live, all it was was just a way for us to carry around goods. Unfortunately, money is inherently countable and can be optimized for. So all hell broke loose bit-by-bit until somehow we’ve ended up at a society that trades money backed on nothing but trust in the country’s institution worth as much or as little as our faith in God. A belief that’s recently being shown on full display in the crypto craze. It’s a system where human lives are just another number on the balance sheet of insurance companies in a crazy bid for the richest, who definitely can’t need more money more than people need their lives, to get the highest returns so that they can watch the numbers on their scoreboard go up. This is part of the meta-game. If we introduce a number and tie it to power, people will try to optimize for this, even to the point of absurdity.
But to even play the meta-game properly we need to get the data and then the means to create an abstracted, simplified view of all of society in a way that we can run it through our pattern finding brains. One would be inclined to tell me this is impossible. But isn’t this precisely what education is? The fact that a load of people understand basic human history, basic economics, mathematics, literature, and more is nothing short of a miracle from this ‘can’t do’ angle. The only problem is that we don’t know what the data for this abstracted worldview is. But this is only part of the problem. If we solve the world today that’s just playing a form of the startup industries of trying to solve the local problem. This isn’t the full meta-game.
The full meta-game comes in when we go into society building. In the creation of societies there are moves that we can make, the creation of cultural heroes and villains, a central narrative, celebrations. America is the ‘city upon a hill’ and ‘the land of the free, home of the brave’ these are myths that identify America. The victory against the British and then the Nazis formed the backbone of the ideas of American justice and freedom for the individual. We celebrate Martin Luther King as a paragon of equality and look to George Washington as the picture of American decency with his apparent inability to even lie. We’ve put capitalism on a pedestal and our tellings of the Cold War with the Soviet Union and their apparently ‘evil’ communism to the point that the word itself feels like it has negative connotations somehow where once the idea itself meant salvation to near slave classes in Europe. Society and its beliefs have building blocks. But why is it important to learn this? Why not just stick to solving our own society? What good is this meta-game?
In a now-famous commencement speech David Foster Wallace tells this small ditty.

“There are these two young fish swimming along and they happen to meet an older fish swimming the other way, who nods at them and says “Morning, boys. How’s the water?” And the two young fish swim on for a bit, and then eventually one of them looks over at the other and goes “What the hell is water?””

This short parable is supposed to show you how hard it is to even see the most important things around you when it has become part of your everyday life, ingrained in your reality and identity. Could you imagine telling a priest of the Spanish Inquisition that maybe killing heretics was a rather ridiculous notion on the grounds that God didn’t exist? God was an absolute to them. Or perhaps to bring it home, that the concept of nations is a rather ridiculous and sub-optimal building block to base your identity around, as this idea of nationalism was started in a big way around the 18th century by those in power in order to indoctrinate you to stay loyal after the whole Enlightenment made it infeasible to smack you with the good-ol divine right of Kings to rule over their people given by God? That this idea was a perfect idea to then brainwash its citizens to their right to glory and start two of the most devastating wars in human history? These are brilliant moves on the part of culture creators, so brilliant that we can no longer even see them as moves and accept them as truths. If we don’t play the meta-game we get stuck again at another local maximum, and then human effort is back again to solving local optimization problems.
Another reason that it’s important to learn the meta-game is simply the fact that if one wants to learn how to impact society, one must know the moves and rules. To paraphrase Wittgenstein, one must know the general rules of chess to meaningfully ask what a ‘king piece’ is. So we must try our hand at this society building over and over and over again in order to understand exactly what it is that’s being done, to learn the rules and the pieces. This is where the linear approximations of realities really shines.
While these are the big moves, we run into another problem. Because we’re creating approximations they run the risk of losing too much important information on the way there. The systems are trying to be objective about life, but this is in itself an impossibility. In The View From Nowhere Nagel points out that trying to achieve any type of objectivity is a kind of paradox. This is because all experience is personal and subjective. Any attempt at a more objective experience is ultimately just a shot at a larger subjective experience. In a similar vein, even with all the objective truth in the world it’s impossible to deny the individual. It would be disingenuous to ask that one forgo one’s interests for some kind of greater good constantly. 
Life has to be lived. This is what Nagel meant when he said that all experience is subjective. Experience can only be self-centered. Similar ideas are encountered in fields such as enactivism where experience itself is said to be embodied, and so having a body is vital to how we experience the world. Nagel has even said that “our own experience provides the basic material for our imagination” in his extremely famous paper What is it like to be a bat?. In the study of language Wittgenstein talks about how language is limited because communicating is like trying to talk about an insect in a box without showing the insect. Even worse, agreeing on what an insect is requires two people doing this at the same time until they just kind of come to an agreement that their ideas seem similar enough. Yet what if this agreement was impossible? What if I had something in my box that you simply didn't? Wittgenstein has an animal thought of his own here where he says “If a lion could talk, we would not understand him”. In short, with such disparate states, we could not even imagine the basic truths that build the ground of these experiences. Since we’re trying to understand people, we won’t run into something as extreme as trying to embody the experience of an echolocating bat or a talking lion. However, trying to understand people from other countries, or socio-economic classes, or even just different jobs has a lot of barriers. Trying to figure out how to efficiently absorb the information from these different experiences will do a lot to increase the basic material for our imagination.
In Andy Weir’s The Egg, the protagonist finds himself in the afterlife talking to a type of god. They find out not only that reincarnation is real, but also that all life in the universe is just him reincarnated over and over again. The reason being that he is being trained for godhood himself. This multitude of human lives is what would be our ultimate goal. It would be the attempt to try to create a type of human singularity with the hope that we could transcend such short-sightedness to create near god-like humans where the abstract problems would become personal ones. Simply, what we think as the limits of our attempts at objectivity would just become the subjective to this being while missing none of the detail. A person who has experienced their own hunger wants food, a person who has experienced a million hungers paired with a million gourmet meals would see the disparity (or so the hope goes). While I have said that it would be disingenuous to ask the individual to forgo one’s own interests for the greater good, here we are hoping that our human singularity would feel the greater good to be their own interest, to feel the big picture personally. For isn’t this what a god is?
It is oddly also a great place to start the whole process. As it’s hard to care about models of reality, but living a life that’s radically different from our own would give us the right tools to ‘see the water’. Everything follows from this. The personalization of a multitude of lives by having lived them, and the ability to iterate through different versions of social structures would give us reason and means to try and approach our reality as something that is both something that can be understood and changed. This is the perfect picture. The question is then, where do we start?
I think we start at the bottom, from the experiences. We must cultivate a generation of people who have true varied perspectives, as this is what drives the need for the rest of the picture. The most dangerous lie is that good is absolute, and that good will find its way to the top somehow. There is no good, only cultivated values. We already have enough food to feed everyone, and the means to house everyone. We have the means to generate and analyze way too much data, and we can go anywhere, talk to anyone. The physical world has been pushed far enough that many of our problems shouldn’t exist, and this is thanks to the age of enlightenment, science, and economy speeding forward with material progress. Now we are by far the weakest link, unable to deal with the complexity of the world we have created. We have everything we need to create a feasible utopia. Now it’s just a problem of having to better ourselves.

Those who know loneliness are the ones who will understand what it means to be lonely. The ones who reach out to help others are the ones who know pain. Perhaps humans are limited in their understanding to see beyond their own experiences; but the fact that they seek to comfort those who are going through the same hardships as they have…. Perhaps that’s where we can see hope.
Hope for mankind.

04/16/2018

	I dislike how my days are going. I’m letting them flow past me without much care. Everyday used to mean so much more to me. It seems to have something to do with attention and want. When one wants something you measure the time pass by one tick at a time, clinging to any sign that the last second, the last minute had left some mark on your mind. Then one gets to the worrisome business of measuring the time left, thinking that maybe if the last minute had left this much then the next minute should leave a little bit more. But when indifference settles, it settles like dust. Filling the grooves of effort painfully etched with the minutes, dulling their edges, softening their corners, until what industry was in the air is now just a shimmer of a million dust particles that swirl in the sunlight. All is slow and time quite immeasurable so that the seconds fade into minutes, and the minutes somehow to days. At first it seems like rest from all the wearisome measuring, but one soon realizes- It is decay.
	So then what does it mean to want for something? Is it the restless nights that just seem to happen as you grind yourself down in the search of a goal? Our ideas about progress seems to have influenced how we conceive ourselves in time. Definitely, my readings of existentialism influenced how I see myself in relations to ideas such as fate. There is no divinity that guides my hand, and so I am utterly alone. Once I understand this, then I am responsible for all my actions. This is what I’ve always thought. But to be responsible does not mean that I am the sole arbiter of the world, it only means that I can only do what I can. So then it becomes a problem of what I want. How does a person ever know what they want?
	There must be a difference between saying ‘I should do something’ and ‘I will do something’.
	However, I can’t keep saying ‘after I do this one thing I’ll live my life’, my life is now, and all of the time I’ll ever receive is already going by, ceaselessly, until I die. Life is now. Life is here. So then what am I doing with all of this life that I’ve gotten? Is it what I want? I don’t think so.
	I will delve deeper into the things I care about: neuroscience, virtual reality, and empathy. I need to constantly hold myself accountable to live within these lines. I am just like all other people, there is nothing special about me. So I must make myself chase the things I want. Write about it, read about it, work on it, meet people who are in it. There are ceaseless opinions and essays on these very topics that I profess myself to be enraptured by. There is no excuse for laziness.

I sat there, staring at the screen, a million little puzzles filling my head. I had to figure out why my http post request was sending out errors, I had to figure out how to order downloads over a network, and I had to look at what was causing tracking errors with my virtual reality headset. It was all on a list, and I had set deadlines for myself. All of it was so… dry. The only real obstacles in my path were time, my own fear of failure, and the allure of a thousand distractions.

What is a dream?

My mind suddenly prompted. It was doing that a lot these days, like a small flashing signal in the back of mind warning me that there was some urgent existential oil change that needed attending to; that my mind was slowly turning into sludge from the accumulation of the everyday annoyances and vapid thoughts that were filtered through.

I felt the stillness of the room again. The books on the bookshelves felt like a little bibliography of my life, gently reminding me of the times I had read them, the cracks along their spines creeping proof of the sleepiness nights that a smaller me had spent escaping to other worlds, knowing with a certainty that only innocence can give that everything was possible.
I press my fingers against my eyes. It sometimes feels like the reward for having a dream is doubt and poor sleep. I feel the old arguments rise, slowly swirling in the background noise of my mind. Nietzche’s eternal recurrence, Sartre’s good faith, Camus’ absurd hero - defense mechanisms that I painstakingly put in place in my early twenties to ensure that I wouldn’t give up on the ideals of my late teens, almost chaining me in place.

Remember the injustice. Remember the guy who got hooked on drugs after everyone abandoned him and telling you about his wonderful acid trip on a bike. Remember the girl who burned all her furniture. Remember the small town girl confiding in a panic to you over a keyboard about her abusive boyfriend. Remember th-

Fuck.
What the hell am I doing.

You’re creating a virtual reality experience that forms a useful tool in the context of the metaverse that allows real time downloading of 3D model using a game engine from the web which-

Shut up.

And this is tied to your long term goal of a user created world based on use and meaning as it frees even the least artistic to create a space like a sandbox to express their inner-

Shut up!

All practiced pitches. Weak pitches. Backed by hope and no figures. There’s another voice in the back of my head echoing the Pareto principle, (only 20 percent of effort is required to get 80 percent of the way there), that I’m missing something and that I should figure out what moves the needle so that I can better use my time. That I should know what the needle is by now. That I’m too slow and that I should be better at big picture thinking. That execution is everything.

My mind brutally beats my thoughts into submission, telling it that there’s no real choice but to sit down and finish at least this small project that I’ve set for myself.
I remember my journal entries for the last few years, demanding action, constructing this weird prison around myself to try and leave me no choice but to keep acting, giving myself no choice in the matter. Some random snippet of something I read years ago flits across my mind, asking me how one can have self discipline if one is beating oneself into submission. Then am I the master or the slave? And how have I done so little?

I dislike thinking. Because I know all the answers that my mind will give me already. I sigh and open my phone, scrolling through conversations, distractions. I haven’t been engaged in a long time. Not when I’m coding, not when I’m talking, not when I’m reading. My entire life feels like it’s being lived through a haze of introspection, my constantly scanning mind somehow blurring the thing that is my life.

'But you seem so miserable'

Ginny. Or my memory of Ginny. An idealized girl that existed nowhere but in my mind for two warm sunny weeks in Wintertime California.

'How will you help people when you yourself are so miserable?'

401 error, authorization. I'm pretty sure I put in the write authorization information, but I know so little that that feeling is worth its weight in thought. I start googling.
But I'm not miserable. I think?

It’s almost been a year. I think it’s odd that we mark the passage of time so much when time itself seems like a continuous concept that keeps flowing on. It feels a little like seeing a river and trying to put marks in the water. But maybe we do this because time feels like it’s tied to our sense of self, as time is tied to our ideas of change. Identity is a tricky thing to define, and so we look at makers- the days, the weeks, the years- in an attempt to grasp at what feels ungraspable.
	I hold little belief in the illusion that you would care about me at all. There are undercurrents of my past in this belief, as people seem to have a knack of not caring about me. But that itself is also a delusion, and I feel that the truth is that people have little time to spare about others who are not central to their lives. To be able to remove the personal feelings out of the equation and try to rationally see the whole picture is also a sign that a person has grown. It’s just another one of the markers we use to try and find ourselves, to define our growth and change.
	So…. time, change, and growth. I guess you can see where this loosely sewn together bit is going. How have you grown, and how have you changed? Are you happier than you were last year? Have you managed to find out if the path you’re pursuing is the one that you’ve always wanted? Are you certain of the meaning that it brings to you life? I ask this because these are the questions that I think are important, and because you seemed rather lost the last time we actually talked. Everyone who talks and opens up to me feels just like that- lost. When they find their way I become less valuable, more disposable. But trying to help people find their way, and catching people before they fall off cliffs, I still believe that there’s value in that.
	Part of me hopes that you are still lost because maybe then there would be something to talk about, something both of us can relate to. But my bigger hope is that you’ve found what you’ve wanted. I believe that you’re a good person, and it’s my hope that you have more than just the run of the mill thoughts. It has always been my wish that people like that could dodge the hardships of both society and existence to grasp at what is beyond the struggle- that thing I like to think of as meaning. If so, would it be possible to tell me what it’s like there?
	Probably nothing special. I know that somewhere in the back of my mind I think that people are not yet capable of even understanding what it means to be alive. Because we’re all so small, and we understand only fragments of the world, and whatever meaning is probably encased in the worldview that you have made for yourself. Such meaning is useless as a reference point for anyone else, and hearing your answer without first putting the effort to understand your worldview would make it sound like nonsense. I do not have the perspective to appreciate your answer, and it’s entirely my fault. After all, it was me who decided to raze even whatever hope we had to building a bridge between us. But I was tired of hurt, and I’d seen that pattern before. Sorry if I was a bit extreme. I wanted the cut, when it eventually happened, to be absolute. My rather horrifying approach was the only way I could think of achieving it, as the cut I wanted was a little different from the stereotypical ‘clean cut’ that people usually refer to. I hope that my actions did not make you jaded in any way. That I am most worried of.

I want to give people a chance to be ‘playful’. But also I want moments where vulnerability is needed. Some way to connect. Not TOO deep, but deep enough. One moment in time. But is it possible to ‘design’ this experience? Feels like I’m trying to make the deepest ice breaking activity ever lol.

’Children of the sky’?

Talking with runes would be too difficult, and I don’t have the time to make a game system like that.

I need a ‘clever’ thing I can make as a weekend project.
I need to create something new, that’s not been tried in XR. I keep saying that I’m one of the best in this field, but I want to prove this.

The other person gets to choose three messages to ‘save’ => I want the space to keep emptying, but I want it to keep the ‘essence’ of what has been said as time passes. How?
The ‘vibes’ should keep updating.
What constitutes a ‘message’? => Don’t worry too much about the tech yet

This doesn’t feel ‘new’ enough. The impact should be front loaded. People should understand the ‘sell’ as fast as possible’
Although a message suddenly being scrawled in front of them would be super cool anyway.

I need to go deeper, not wider.

I need to make it easier to ‘add’ the person as a friend. 

Make an app that would move ME. Not anyone else, just me.

This tribute I write for the child who tried as hard as he could to change a situation that he was powerless to change. He hadn’t still understood that his heart was even frailer than his small body, and so he beat it against rocks. He was one full of laughter, and embarrassingly sensitive; one who wanted to cry at the small injustices. He thought that if he tried as hard as he could, he could change everything around him. After all, why shouldn’t he be able to? Everything he had read, everybody that he had talked to, they all seemed to affirm the belief that his words should matter to someone. If there was anyone that his words should matter to it was his family. So he gave up all the small pleasures. Pleasures like being able to go outside whenever he wanted, to dawdle a little after school to talk to his classmates, and the pleasure to read uninterrupted on his bed as he fell deeper and deeper into books.
He felt he was worth something. That was his mistake, or at least that’s what was incompatible with his surroundings. Especially after the move, everything was horrible. Every single day upon crossing the doorway he was in fight-or-flight. Every small conversation could stray into an argument. Arguments that were so one sided, where his voice wasn’t heard. But his voice SHOULD be heard. He had read enough, had thought enough, and he thought that he’d seen quite a bit too. But at least it should be enough to explain, just to explain what he was thinking when he had said a sentence, or why he didn’t like taking constant orders. But orders were to be obeyed, and anyway something had annoyed her a little today, and the rules were even tighter than usual. The boy, the boy, the boy he just wanted to be heard. His anger boiling over to rage. Coming up with stupid systems where maybe he could talk and then she could talk, and they could eventually come to some understanding. Some way forward. But no. No. It was always ‘why can’t you’, ‘why aren’t you more like’, ‘you shitty brat’, ‘is it because you’re so dumb you can’t’, ‘we sacrifice so much’, ‘I hope you have kids like you one day that destroy your life’… If only he could TALK. If only he could be heard in this hellhole of a place.
Well he had a little sister who was afraid and hurt too. So he wanted to keep laughing and smiling. But the rage just kept building. He was hard done by. He was certain. If he wasn’t hard done by, none of this made any sense. Why one earth was he so alone. Why did no one listen? Who does he turn to when times get rough? When, oh god, does he get to sit down and feel sorry about himself and have a good cry?

Hey VR peeps, I'm just posting this to share some general insights into VR I've had over the years. Feels like it could be useful for people who are actually thinking with some more depth about VR. I just miss these kinds of convos I guess. If anybody has any leads to where I can find these kinds of communities lmk!

Well the tl;dr is that by actually only tracking our head and hands, a bunch of really weird things happens to how we can think about our bodies and how we use them to interact with the environment in VR.

----------------------------

Commercial VR sets today come with a head mounted display (HMD) and two controllers. Usually for reasons of presence, VR experiences give us some kind of body. But these bodies aren’t real, and are usually rigged with some kind of inverse kinematics (IK). For those who don’t know, inverse kinematics is just taking a bunch of joints and figuring out where they are based on where some other joints are, and constraints on how much the joints can bend. In VR that means that the software takes the position of your head and hands and then fits the whole body depending on those, knowing basic stuff like your elbows shouldn’t bend outwards. This is why in VR you sometimes get your avatar’s elbows sticking out to your sides, the program is just guessing wrong.

But what all this means is that your body isn’t really there, what’s actually there is just your head and your hands. But it’s not really your had and your hands, they’re just anchor points that give a reference of position as to roughly where your head and hands are.

Why is this important?

Well, for different reasons. In VR, your head is usually used as a point of reference as to where your character’s location actually is. This can lead to some oddly tricky situations where you’re peeking over a cliff or around a corner, but your whole body is moved.

The game engine can’t really tell the difference between these as long as only the head and hands are tracked. The illustrations above make this problem more obvious (while also showing you how bad I draw).

But it should be pretty obvious now that VR avatars, as they are set up right now, aren’t the best at finicky poses. This makes genres such as stealth, much more difficult than one would like. As actions such as sticking to walls and peeking around corners aren’t guaranteed to work.

In general, this means that inputs (with inputs here being the literal positioning of your body) might not work the way that players want them to. And we all know that games mis-inputting commands is extremely frustrating. Since we want the player to feel like they have control over their own body at all times, this is an important design constraint.

The problem of precise movement gets even worse with hands.

In real life, we actually require extremely precise movements from our hands very frequently. We also rely on a bunch of different stimuli to perform tasks involving our hands successfully. Even for things we really don’t think are that complicated.

For example, when we pick up a cup full of water we first need to feel the cup on our skin. The tactile feeling of the cup on our skin, as well as the resistance that the weight of the cup gives gives us precise signals as to how to move to envelop the cup with our palm and fingers without toppling it over or pushing it away. The resistance offered by the shape of the cup itself helps us to know when to stop closing our fingers. If we didn’t have these signals we would either just keep constricting our grip until the glass shatters in our hand, or we would grab too loosely and drop the cup when we tried to pick it up. Then when we pick the cup up, the combined weight of the cup and its contents helps us know just how much strength to put in to lifting the cup. The shifting center of weight helps us to keep angling the cup as we lift it so as to avoid spilling its contents. This lack of weight and acceleration of objects is also why throwing objects in VR usually feels terrible.

All of this is just not possible with the current control scheme in VR. Even with hand tracking there is no tactile feedback or resistance offered by objects. While there are people working on this, I’ll stick to what we got for this discussion.

So as I said, grabbing objects is hard. Any number of movements that require precise movements is hard. If we look at the grabbing portion of the cup example above, what happens looks something like this.

But this is obviously impossible with the control scheme that we have in VR right now. What happens in VR when we grab objects is pretty much this.

Our hands actually aren’t hands. They’re too limited. The hands are actually an illusion, and it’s easier to think of them as spheres with button inputs to perform specific actions.

People have come up with various clever ways of using the oculus controllers to do various things. One basic way is thinking about the oculus controller as a handle for whatever virtual object that you’re using. This has been used for swords and guns a lot. Like a LOT. Also ping pong paddles a surprising amount of times.

The lightsaber, gun, and ping pong paddle are also great objects to be holding because they require much less feedback. For example, a real sword would make you expect a pretty big torque force from the blade to your handle, but you would only expect a light vibration from the lightsaber as you’d expect it to just cut through things with ease. The gun is also an object that can kind of make do with vibrations from the controller for kickback, and ping pong balls are not really known for their massive weight. Bow and arrow is also a popular object in VR for similar reasons.

One other very early thing that people figured out was using a type of ‘laser’ that came out from the front of the controller. This was used to select objects far away, and is pretty much a gun again. Tilt Brush also uses the point just in front of the controller to draw with, like the tip of your pen. Kind of like a very very short laser if you think about it.

VR does try to use the hand mesh/object itself to act as more than just spherical blobs in space and tries to introduce more natural hand movements and inputs in some pretty cool ways.

The Oculus Touch uses capacitive sensors on its buttons to tell if the person has their hands on the buttons, which then translates to various hand… postures(?). Is there a word for that? Gestures?

Anyway, these can then be used for some more natural gestures. Like, I’m pretty sure everyone has done finger guns and thumbs up in VR. I’ll show some of the most used possible hand gestures below. The pic is a bit old, but the ideas have stayed pretty much the same.

You can actually use these as distinct inputs, such as the thumbs up triggering a like. There is also a pretty neat use-case in Neos VR where a game lets you make a frame with your thumbs and index fingers to take a picture.

The Valve Index controllers go a little bit further than the oculus controllers, in that it just has a strip on the part of the controller that you grab that can sense if your fingers are on it or not. Also, it can sense if you’re actually grabbing an object as opposed to just having your fingers down.

I feel that this is a somewhat better solution than the Oculus Quest’s solution of simply including finger tracking. This is because while hand tracking does feasibly give us better accuracy, the accuracy is wasted because we can’t really do anything that requires that much accuracy because of the whole ‘lack of tactile feedback and resistance’ thing that I mentioned in the cup example. Imagine trying to button a shirt without the buttons pushing back at you. That might actually be a new level of hell.

The Valve Index controllers also have the advantage of being able to actually grab your controller when you grab objects. This helps with immersion when you’re grabbing your sword/gun/ping pong paddle, as opposed to just grabbing thin air.

Of course, there are probably use cases where the hand tracking is more useful than the Valve Index controllers, but I haven’t quite seen much yet. You could argue for specific hand gestures for specific inputs, but that sounds like a huge headache to figure out when to accept the inputs. Also, making sure of the inputs probably puts you in around the same ballpark as what you would have been able to achieve with the Valve Index controllers anyway.

Of course, the hand mesh itself can still be used in VR. We can use the hand object to push buttons, and it’s a pretty common thing to use your index fingers to press a button. However, the problem still stands that we can’t track minute movements with much reliability, and that button inputs in real life rely on the object’s ability to push back. For example, imagine if your fingers simply phased through your keyboard. You wouldn’t be able to have your fingers slide along your keys as you typed, you would have to manually stop your fingers as opposed to pushing down and letting the keyboard itself just hold them, and you wouldn’t be able to rest your hands on the keyboard or table itself.

All of this translates to huge buttons in VR to compensate.

Of course, there are ways to bring your keyboard with you into the virtual environment now, but for the most part this is what people are dealing with.

The other way of interacting with the virtual environment is motion controls. Motion controls are actually much more common than you think. This is because the act of swinging a sword, aiming your gun, pulling back a bowstring, throwing an object, etc are all motion controls. People just kind of don’t really think of these as motion controls because these are extremely natural. This is kind of what part of the magic of virtual reality is, and a huge part of the immersive experience.

In my head, there are two other types of motion controls other than the purely natural ones. The first is motion controls that are kind of natural, but ones we wouldn’t really do in real life. I’m talking about things such as flapping your arms to fly, or using your arms to walk, swinging with grappling hooks, etc. These are all in virtual reality in games such as Birdly, Gorilla Tag, and Windlands respectively, and they allow us to intuite natural movements that we usually wouldn’t have any reason to execute.

The third type of motion control is the one that most people would think of when talking about motion controls. This is the one where you perform strange arbitrary actions to make things happen.

One game that does this pretty well is Waltz of the Wizard : Natural Magic. This article from the Road to VR explains it best. I’ll quote from it.

“You can blast out the particles from both hands to get the most destructive shot—simply pull your palms towards you while grabbing to ‘gather’ magical particles and then release to shoot them out. If you toss them out with a quick motion, they’re powerful and compact. Toss them out slowly, and the particles gently leave your hands and spread apart for a wider area of effect… Those particles can be guided in mid-air by holding the trigger again and moving your hand; you can move around corners, chase flying enemies, and navigate your shot through tight spaces like windows… By slowing down and directing your shot mid-flight, you can also cover baddies with particles and telekinetically control them”.

All of this is really, really cool. But they’re also contrived. You’re literally creating a new language in VR that’s absolutely native to the experience. Another VR game that’s playing around with the idea in a cool way is Rumble, which is trying to recreate something akin to earth bending from the Avatar series.

This type of interaction, when done well, can push forward what is possible for us as human beings. It adds new grammar to what we can do with our bodies.

For the last part of this I want to actually look at the bodies that we actually have.

In VR, as I’ve said before, we only have our heads and our hands. We can’t really fully ignore the fact that we have legs, they take somewhat of a backseat to what we do usually have in VR. The actual body that you have in VR usually feels a little like this.

 Where are our feet and elbows?! (long post)

Well you don’t quite feel electricity flowing through your arms. But it’s more like your head and your arms are tentatively linked to your center chest area. Everything else, the game engine can get wrong (as I showed in the first drawing with your elbows sticking out). I tried to show this rather shifty nature of the position of your arms with lightning.

Nothing really properly exists below that chest point in VR unless you buy extra trackers. There are some cases where you need to squat down where this action does afford you some more presence, but that’s just your real body compensating for what virtual reality can’t do. Your body plus the movement of your camera is sometimes enough to trick you.

So now it becomes more obvious why facebook decided to just lop off your legs in Facebook Horizons.

Big name VR experiences such as Rec Room and Orbus actually take it one step further and do away with your arms entirely.

This is pretty interesting when we’re trying to approximate being a person in-game. But that’s a top-down approach. In other words, we want to be human and then we work with what we got.

What if we worked the other way? The bottom-up approach here would be to take what we got and then see what we can do with this. I believe that this could lead to more intuitive and natural interactions in VR. For instance, I mentioned Gorilla Tag earlier. Gorilla Tag is a hilarious game where the basic premise is ‘what if your arms WERE your legs?’, and then you run away or chase other gorillas by swinging your arms back and forth like a gorilla. You can even climb up things by grabbing them, fully making locomotion only hand based. Which is extremely natural and intuitive.

This kind of leveraging of what VR offers and then recontextualizing it into a situation that works might be a more fun avenue to go down than just trying to make human avatars with what we have. Any in-game character that only has a head, torso, and two hands can work.

This is a first pass look at user input in VR, it’s shortcomings, and some ways it’s been played with by developers.

Of course full body tracking gets rid of a lot of these insights, but it's just a note on what's been happening up until this point. Also, feel free to just hmu for a chat or comment on whatever. I just love VR lol

I'm not a frequenter of this subreddit, but I just saw the ' People who look down on someone who read for entertainment.' thread on the front page, and found it somewhat unsettling. I hope I'm not beating a dead horse by making this post. I would also hope that I'm not assuming too much by voicing my opinion, but I'm afraid that that ship has probably sailed AND sunk in some spectacular fashion. But I want to give my story.

I want to start off by saying that I was an avid reader during my adolescent years, and I completely understand the joys of reading for nothing but pleasure. I started off, as many have, with Harry Potter. I read LotR, some disc world, lots of Roald Dahl, Enid Blyton (I grew up in the UK during my early reading years), Time Twister, lots of Garth Nix, Dragonlance, Dan Brown blah blah blah. I've even read the Twilight series, Divergent series, and other YA stuff even when I was in my later teens. I read historical fiction books like Emperor (Julius Ceasar) and a series on Genghis Khan. From 11-13 I think I was reading at least a hundred books a year. That slowed down due to a move to Korea and a focus on studies. The books I have listed are what I can remember off the top of my head, and are by no means exhaustive. So I really, REALLY get what it feels like to read for fun.

But I remember one day when I tried to get some other book (I think it was 'The Fall of Gondolin' since I love Tolkien), and my dad just looked at me and said "This is fine, but you should think about broadening your horizons a bit". He still let me get it of course, and it was great fun reading about the Battle of Unnumbered Tears after only having fleetingly read about it in the Silmarillion. But his words kinda stuck with me.

So I tried my hand at the classics. I'd completed some stuff from Charlotte Bronte and Dickens before, but honestly they were too hard for me at the time. This is what dissuaded me from classics for a looooong time. Since I got the idea that they were a tad stuffy, and didn't really GO anywhere. But since my dad had nudged me a bit, and since I trusted him I tried my hand at 'A Christmas Carol'. It was kinda great, and that surprised me.

After I closed the book, I remembered an argument I heard my parents having back when I was reading all those books at 12-ish. My mother was a classic tiger asian mum, and wanted me to read harder books (and thus the first poke into classics). My dad didn't like this idea and said it could turn me off reading, that there was an age to these kind of things. At the time I didn't care too much about what was being argued over, and I was just happy that I got to keep reading about Australian time guardians who were prophesied to become gods. The only lasting influence it had on me at that time was that it felt odd that books would have an 'age' to read them at. Since weren't all books a great romp? How could someone read a book and not GET it?

That question got answered after I read 'A Christmas Carol'. These questions about morality and greed seemed to make more sense to me than when I read it when I was younger. Then I read Oliver Twist, and the plight of a child much like me trying to keep it together in a hostile and confounding environment while horrible things happened was also oddly relatable. Lord of the Flies was great since I was at that edgy time where I looked around and through that everyone was a monster and this book was totally like 'yeah, totes, beelzebub'. I got into Shakespeare and I loved 'Julius Caesar' and the sheer drama of it all. I absolutely ADORED Hamlet, since that indecision about life is exactly what I was feeling as I geared up for college. 'The Stranger' made me understand that crazy disconnect i felt with a world that seemed to want me to conform to its social norms. When I opened Harry Potter again, it was there, like an old friend. But it was a friend I'd long since outgrown. The themes of friendship and perseverance were still there, but it was now so naive and innocent. It was a book that I would love my kids to read as they tentatively step into literature.

But as I kept reading I felt that there were only so many fantasy romps you could read before feeling like there were only so many variants of the same tropes that you could take (The Belgariad anyone?), and that I was just reading the same tweaks of stories over and over and over again. There's nothing wrong with this, it's the same as bingeing shows like Parks and Rec or Merlin on TV. But after a while it's just that, bingeing. If that's all you want from books, then great, you've found a solution to a problem you had- namely entertainment.

However, if I were ever to have a kid who I wished the best for I think I would do the same as my dad did. I would let them indulge in whatever they liked, but I'd nudge them in directions that might challenge them. Since there is much MUCH more value you could get out of books and the time spent reading than just reading the next installation of 'you're secretly special and here's why, also swords and sex'.

There is so much more to life, and books are treasure troves. They're amazing repositories of experience that people have put together in the hope that they would help someone understand some corner of life that they thought was worth dedicating their lives to. Entertainment is great, and I read weekly manga as a habit from my teenage years in Korea. But I also read Woolf, and following her along on her weird trotting of thoughts that paints a picture of life is so... precious. Trying to piece together Dostoevsky's nihilism is sometimes utterly terrifying and still hopeful. There are questions they induce in you that I think make life a little bit more interesting, and slightly more full of worth. This is why I always try to see if I can get people to read more difficult books, and it's why I try to read more difficult books (and I have a long way to go).

I would never look down on people who are still reading for entertainment. But there is a deep frustration that's felt when someone reading something like 'The Name of the Wind' tries to argue it has equal literary merit as compared to something like JR by Gaddis. Not because I'm trying to gatekeep, but because there's just SO. MUCH. LIFE. that's being missed in this statement. But these are things I only really feel with my friends. Because I KNOW that if they could just crack open a more 'difficult' (heavy air quotes) book they could find so much more there. I recently finally got a friend to read 'The Idiot', and they're enamoured. They said they loved how the characters seem to really try and talk to each other, and that the way that the prince disarms everyone with his innocence reminds him of himself and how he tries so hard to maintain what seems to come naturally for this character.

Books can be difficult, but a lot of people miss the point entirely and use this difficulty to try and set themselves apart as 'true readers'. It's no wonder there's huge blowback because of these types of approaches to getting people to read. Books are about life, and experiences, and beliefs, and of course it's going to be difficult to convey these things. There's going to be several styles that people have tried when trying to convey this desperation of life and beauty. It's NOT the difficulty and the 'status' that people seem to think that reading such books confers them that should be the focus, it's the sharing of life and ideas that should be considered.

There's a book called 'Rights of the Reader' by Pennac that I absolutely loved (and gave away to a friend as a going away present), and there was this bit that I really liked about a Professor who would walk into the classroom and just read a book to his students. He would not expect any of them to come with knowledge of the greats of literature, but would just offer up these books as a stand-alone gift. He said (I'm heavily paraphrasing) that it was a shame to have to read books like this in a room. That to read was to want to go with Kierkegaard and rage against his father about life and God, and to look up at the pointed roofs of churches and try to figure out the point of life itself. Sadly, the book is the best (if poor) substitute. So they can only but share it and converse with each other.

This has become a bit long, and I apologize if this has become a bit preachy... but I dunno. I just feel a bit strongly about this whole 'why read classics' thing that seems so prevalent.
